def: A measure of how much an estimate, such as an eval score, would vary if the sampling of questions were repeated.
The estimate plus or minus 1.96 standard errors: a range built so that about 95 percent of intervals made this way contain the true value.
The hypothetical, unlimited set of questions from which an eval's questions are treated as a random sample.
A confidence interval for a proportion that behaves sensibly for small samples and scores near 0 or 100 percent.
The spread of a single question's scores around its own pass rate, caused by randomness in the model's answers.
Answering each question K times and averaging, which shrinks answer-level noise by a factor of K but not the noise from choosing questions.
A standard error that treats groups of related questions as the independent units, so correlated questions do not overstate precision.
Estimating an interval by recomputing the score on many pseudo-evals made by resampling the independent units with replacement.
The per-question difference between two systems' scores on the same questions, used so shared difficulty cancels out of the comparison.
The probability that an eval detects a real difference of a given size.
The smallest true difference between two systems that an eval of a given size would detect with a stated power and false-positive rate.
The inflation of false positives that occurs when many slices, metrics or variants are tested and the best-looking one is reported.
